sections.html:
Jefferson Parish is the suburban ring west and south of New Orleans, cut in two by the Mississippi. The 2020 census counted 440,781 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 431,398. Of the parish's 665 square miles, only 296 are land. Residents talk about it in two halves: East Jefferson (Metairie, Kenner, Harahan) and the West Bank (Gretna, Harvey, Marrero, Westwego). Much of the housing went up in the postwar subdivision boom, so plenty of houses are now old enough that roofs, wiring and drainage can slow a financed sale.

sections.h2: Who sends the bill and who sets the value
sections.html:
The job is divided between two offices. The Assessor decides what your property is worth. The Sheriff mails the bill and takes your payment. Both Assessor offices keep hours 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Sheriff's office collects as ex-officio tax collector, and its website lets you pay property taxes online, with a separate module for homestead and mortgage-company payments.

Homes are assessed at 10% of fair market value. Voters approve millage and a local ordinance sets it, and the tax is that millage rate applied to the assessed value. A home inside a city such as Kenner or Gretna pays several levies at once: the parish, the school board, the city and possibly special districts. Whatever name is on your mailing address, the same offices handle your bill.

The Assessor has to send every assessment change to the Louisiana Tax Commission for approval, which makes the Commission the final administrative stop in a value dispute.

Payment is expected as soon as the notice lands, and a bill turns delinquent after December 31. The 2025 bills went delinquent on December 31, 2025, and a short grace window for payments made or postmarked just after that ran to January 2, 2026. Go by the date on your own notice, since the calendar can move it.

Late bills pick up interest at 1% per month, counted from January 1 until you pay. If you mail a check, a postmark proves you were on time, but getting that postmark on the envelope before the deadline is your problem, not the Sheriff's.

  • The Sheriff takes partial payments, though interest and extra costs (certified mail, advertisements, mortgage certificate fees) keep adding up on the balance.
  • Pay in full before the June tax sale.
  • After several years of unpaid taxes, the sale process can move ownership.
  • If a tax sale does happen, the former owner has three years after it is recorded to buy the property back. The payoff is the sale price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest (see this Attorney General opinion).

Go to the Assessor while the rolls are open for inspection. Once that period ends, the appeal form says, no assessment can be changed. Under R.S. 47:1992.1 the rolls stay open for fifteen calendar days. It opens on or after August 1 and shuts by September 15.

The form is strict. Submit all the requested information, because an incomplete form is denied. You need enough documentation to show the assessment may be wrong, and the office makes no promise to agree to a change.

  • Photos must show the whole structure as seen from the street. Interior damage photos must show the entire room. Photocopied photos are refused.
  • You can attach repair estimates, an appraisal or a letter explaining your case.
  • If you are not the owner, a Tax Authorization Form must accompany the request.
  • File one form per property. The apartment form adds a request for two prior calendar years of income and expense statements, plus occupancy rates.

If the Assessor will not budge, take it to the parish Board of Review. You can appeal that ruling to the Louisiana Tax Commission. Call the Assessor each summer for current Board of Review filing dates.

Sign up in person at either Assessor office. You will need your act of sale and a photo ID that shows the home's address. If a married couple owns the house together, one spouse can go alone.

Louisiana's constitution takes the first $7,500 of assessed value off the bill for state, parish and special taxes. That equals $75,000 of fair market value. Once you file, you get a yearly receipt in the mail confirming the exemption stays in place. The Assessor's site also carries separate applications for first responders and volunteer firefighters, with a September 1 filing cutoff for the current tax year.

Your exemption stops when you sell. The next owner, if living there, must file a fresh claim after closing, and the first paper the Assessor asks that person for is the deed.

Hurricane Katrina, which made landfall on August 29, 2005, is the reference point buyers and insurers use. The East Bank saw widespread flooding and wind damage, while the West Bank had little to no flooding but plenty of wind damage. Jefferson's levees and floodwalls did not fail, so floodwater could be pumped out quickly.

The parish Department of Floodplain Management and Hazard Mitigation (504-736-6540) can tell you whether a lot sits in a regulated flood zone. If a storm has lowered your home's condition, document it. The appeal form asks for repair estimates and photos, and a damaged house can support a lower valuation during the inspection window.

A tax bill you have not paid will not stop a sale. The balance comes out of your proceeds at the table. Outside New Orleans, anyone party to an act of sale can ask for a certificate that shows which state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are still unpaid. The sale year itself is excluded (R.S. 9:2901).

The transfer then has to be recorded. Under Civil Code article 3338, a transfer of land does not bind outsiders until it sits in the conveyance records. So the closing attorney or title company files the act with the clerk promptly.

Here is the usual order of events:

  1. Ask the Sheriff's office what is owed on the bill, including interest and costs.
  2. The title company orders the tax certificate.
  3. You sign the act of sale before a notary, and back taxes are deducted from what you receive.
  4. The closing agent records the act. The buyer then files a homestead claim of their own.

If you have back taxes, a storm-damaged roof or a tenant, a buyer who takes the house as-is can be the simpler route. The Sheriff also publishes a list of judicial real estate sales. Look at it if a lender or creditor has already moved against the property.

faqs.q: What office collects property tax in Jefferson Parish?
faqs.a: The Jefferson Parish Sheriff collects it as ex-officio tax collector. The Assessor, with offices in Gretna and Harahan, sets the value, and the Louisiana Tax Commission approves assessment changes.

faqs.q: What is the interest on late Jefferson Parish property tax?
faqs.a: Interest runs at 1% per month from January 1 until the bill is paid. Partial payments are accepted, but interest and costs such as certified mail and advertising keep building.

faqs.q: When can I dispute my Jefferson Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Only during the open-rolls period, which lasts fifteen calendar days, beginning no earlier than August 1 and ending no later than September 15. After it closes, no assessment changes can be made.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Jefferson Parish house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The taxes are paid from the proceeds at closing, and a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901 shows what is outstanding. A cash buyer who closes as-is can still complete the purchase.

faqs.q: Where do I file for a homestead exemption in Jefferson Parish?
faqs.a: In person at either Assessor office, at 200 Derbigny St. in Gretna or 1221 Elmwood Park Blvd. in Harahan. Bring your act of sale and a photo ID showing the home address.
